subject: RFI: Inference runtime network segregation and threat walkthrough

Subject: RFI: Inference runtime network segregation and threat walkthrough

Hi Dylan,

Thanks for engaging on our RFI. As part of our security review for vendor inference platforms we need a concise network and threat walkthrough that covers the following:

- A high-level network diagram showing control plane, inference runtime, GPU worker pools, and customer connectivity options (hosted API, dedicated, private VPC/on-prem).
- How you enforce tenant isolation at the network and process level (VPCs, subnets, hypervisor/host isolation, container boundaries).
- Egress and ingress controls (firewall rules, NAT, firewall-as-code), and whether customer traffic traverses shared routing.
- Sidecar/mTLS and service mesh approaches for control-plane to runtime communication.
- Key hardening measures for the inference runtime (KV cache isolation, model artifacts signing, kernel hardening, quantized model integrity checks).
- Threat model summary for lateral movement, data exfiltration from running inference, and supply-chain risks (model weights and container images).

Can you send a short diagram and a 1-2 page threat summary we can attach to the RFP package? Also indicate whether you support hosting inside our VPC (VPC peering, private deployment) and if there are any known operational constraints.

Please reply with attachments or a link to a secured drive.

Thanks,
Jane Doe
Acme Corp — Security Engineering
security@acme-corp.com

Attachment: acme_rfi_requirements_v1.pdf

Subject: Re: RFI: Inference runtime network segregation and threat walkthrough

Jane — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Monica (platform security) and Grace (product) to make sure we capture operational constraints.

Quick summary up front: yes, we support all three deployment modes you listed (hosted API, Dedicated/reserved GPU pools, and Private — VPC and on-prem). For regulated customers we typically recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) where traffic and data plane are fully under customer network controls.

Attached are:
- redwood_inference_inference_vpc_diagram_v1.png (high-level diagram)
- threat_model_summary_acme_v1.pdf (2-page summary with mitigations)
- config-snippets.txt (examples: FIPS TLS, mTLS policy, egress deny-by-default snippet)

Highlights from the threat summary (pulled from the PDF):
- Tenant isolation: network layer uses dedicated subnets per-customer in Dedicated; hosted uses strict namespace + macvlan-like overlay + network policy to isolate tenant pods. Runtime enforces process isolation by running each model session inside an ephemeral sandboxed container; KV caches are namespaced with per-tenant keys and access tokens are short-lived.
- Control plane communications: mTLS (mutual TLS) with cert rotation via our CA service for internal services; control-plane -> runtime uses a control channel authenticated with short-lived client certs and signed requests (HMAC + nonce).
- Egress/ingress controls: default deny egress for inference workers; explicit egress rules only for telemetry and model fetching (signed artifact endpoints). VPC deployments can use TGW (transit gateway) or VPC peering depending on customer preference. For private/on-prem we support air-gapped installs — model artifacts are loaded via signed bundles and local KMS/HSM integration.
- KV cache & secret handling: KV cache entries are segregated per deployment and encrypted at rest with separate DEKs per-customer. DEKs are wrapped with customer or Redwood-managed KMS. We recommend customer-managed KMS for high-compliance customers.
- Supply chain: we sign model files and container images; runtime verifies signature before loading. Build pipeline enforces SBOM generation and image provenance checks.

Operational constraints:
- Private on-prem installs require a maintenance window for kernel/firmware patches — we provide an orchestrated patch plan; some older GPUs require node-level reboot for certain microcode updates.
- VPC peering imposes route table limits in some cloud accounts — our onboarding team pre-validates route counts.

Next steps: Monica, can you confirm the VPC peering options and provide the concrete CIDR recommendations? Grace, can you confirm whether the signed-model workflow docs are acceptable for Acme's procurement?

Regards,
Dylan Brooks
Senior Sales Engineer — Redwood Inference
redwood.ai

Thanks Dylan — received the attachments and the summary looks good at a high level. A couple of follow-ups: 

1) For hosted API customers, you mention "namespace + macvlan-like overlay + network policy." Can you expand on how the overlay prevents ARP/Layer2 leakage between tenants, and whether you use host-level ebtables/nftables rules vs pure CNI enforcement?

2) Regarding signed model files: do you support per-tenant model signing keys (customer-supplied key material) or only Redwood-managed signing?

3) For private VPC: can you confirm whether your control plane needs inbound routes from the customer VPC, or if control-plane traffic is only outbound to Redwood-managed endpoints? We need to map firewall rules accordingly.

We're aiming to finalize the security annex by EOD Thursday — appreciate any clarifications.

Thanks,
Jane

Jane — thanks for the specific questions. Short answers below, with pointers to the attached config-snippets.txt for concrete policy examples.

1) Layer 2 leakage and overlay enforcement:
- For hosted and dedicated we use a combination: CNI-enforced micro-segmentation (NetworkPolicy for L3/L4) plus host-level bridge isolation. We disable promiscuous mode on host interfaces and enforce ebtables/nftables rules at the host when needed to block gratuitous ARP and prevent MAC spoofing between tenant endpoints. Our overlay is engineered so that tenant MACs are not injected into the host bridge — traffic is tunneled with per-tenant encapsulation identifiers.
- We also run periodic ARP/NDP anomaly detection (agent telemetry) and will quarantine nodes when anomalies exceed thresholds.

2) Model signing keys:
- We support both modes. Customers can bring their own signing keys (BYOK) and configure our artifact registry to accept only artifacts signed by the customer key. Alternatively, Redwood-managed signing is available; in that case, keys are stored in a customer-specific key slot in KMS and rotation policies are customer-configurable. The signed-model verification happens in the runtime before mapping a model into GPU memory.

3) Control plane routing for Private VPC:
- Default: control-plane is outbound-only from the customer's VPC to a Redwood-managed control endpoint (HTTPS mTLS). This keeps firewall rules simple (allow outbound to specific FQDNs/IPs and ports).
- Optionally: for higher-throughput Dedicated connections we can establish a persistent peering/tunnel where the customer's network peers with our control plane; that requires inbound allow rules on the peering side (we provide a minimal set of IP ranges and ports during onboarding). We provide per-onboarding CIDR recommendations and a pre-check script.

Operational note: when customers choose BYOK for model signing and customer-managed KMS, we recommend a short onboarding window to exchange trust material and test a signed artifact deployment in a staging environment.

If you want, I can schedule a 30-minute tech deep-dive with our infra team and the Acme network/security architects. We can include the concrete ebtables snippets and a traceback demo for ARP anomaly quarantine.

Best,
Monica Patel
